summary:
Gangwon province stands under the national framework of South Korea: gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and no province-specific ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans visitors is documented in these sources. The rules a visitor meets in Gangwon are the national ones.

Legal gender recognition no longer depends on surgery. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that determining gender change by surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery are now reference only, not criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live according to their gender identity. That ruling is the standard applied in Gangwon, where no province-specific case is documented. The Supreme Court has separately allowed a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 a Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award against a claim of 3 million won, ruling that police advice telling a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights. The court held comfortable restroom use to be a fundamental and universal human right. A 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) award of 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a transgender student from its restroom forms part of the national standard applied in Gangwon, where no specific incident is documented.

Restroom avoidance is a documented national pattern rather than a local one. A 2021 National Human Rights Commission of Korea survey of 591 transgender respondents found 41% used a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoided food and drink to do so, and 36% forwent restroom use entirely.

The armed forces are the exception to South Korea's non-criminalisation: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld it in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether. This bears on a visitor only insofar as it applies to nationals serving, not to civilians.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity in South Korea, so accommodation, services and employment carry no statutory protection on these grounds. The National Human Rights Commission flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023 after the Ministry of Health and Welfare refused to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

No same-sex marriage exists, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner; the Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extended recognition only to same-sex partners' healthcare rights. Organised conservative opposition remains active, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in South Korea alongside a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
tangentialFactors:
The strongest documented friction for a trans visitor in Gangwon concerns public restrooms, but the evidence is national: police advice to avoid women's restrooms was ruled an infringement of personal rights in 2024, and a beauty academy was ordered to pay 7 million won in 2021 for the same conduct. Neither case arose in Gangwon, and no local incident is recorded there.

South Korea's trajectory on trans legal rights is judicial rather than legislative. Courts have removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and have awarded damages against the state for restroom advice, while the legislature has produced no anti-discrimination statute. Visitors should expect protections that hold when litigated but do not operate as standing administrative rules.

Social friction is organised rather than diffuse. Conservative groups contest LGBT visibility publicly, and the Ministry of Health and Welfare's refusal to draft transgender hospitalisation guidelines in 2023 shows administrative resistance continuing even as courts move the other way.

Gangwon's own record contributes no data point: no province-specific ordinance, case or enforcement pattern appears in the sources, so the province reads as an instance of the national picture rather than a distinct one.

There is no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, services or accommodation. Hospitalisation guidance for transgender patients has not been drafted; the Ministry of Health and Welfare declined the request in November 2023 and the National Human Rights Commission flagged the gap that same period.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources record no Gangwon-specific ordinance, police practice, court case or violent incident involving a trans person; the province-level characterisation rests on absence of documentation rather than on a surveyed local record, and remains unresolved.

The Yeongdong ruling of 8 May 2024 and the Seoul appellate restroom judgment of July 2024 are described by wire and press accounts; the full texts of both judgments are not in the inventory, so the precise scope of the holdings is unverified here.

The National Human Rights Commission survey of 591 transgender respondents is reported second-hand from 2021, with no sampling detail available in these sources.

Whether the 7 million won Pohang-branch award and the 300,000 won Seoul award have prompted changes in police or school guidance in Gangwon is not sourced.

Facilities, healthcare access and documentation practice for a foreign trans visitor entering Gangwon, as distinct from a Korean national changing registered sex, are not addressed in the inventory.
